summary: Introduces the set of DNS Security Extensions in one place and points to the main RFCs that define them. It states that using DNSSEC for origin authentication of DNS data is the best current practice. It does not update the earlier DNSSEC documents.

plainLanguage.summary: DNSSEC puts a tamper-proof seal on internet address-book answers so you know they were not faked. This document is a map to all the pieces.

questions: what are the dnssec core documents
subtitle: A roadmap to the many RFCs that make up DNSSEC, and a statement that using it is best current practice.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC is spread across many RFCs, and implementers, operators and other documents have no single place that lists them or says what status DNSSEC has.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9364 lists the core documents (RFC 4033, RFC 4034, RFC 4035 and RFC 6840), the added algorithms, the extensions and other useful documents, and declares DNSSEC the best current practice for origin authentication of DNS data. It does not update any of them.
tldr.outcome: It serves as a single reference for DNSSEC. The text admits deployment is limited, saying fewer than 10% of website domain names were signed, but holds that this does not change the best-current-practice status.

today: RFC 9364 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 237) and has not been obsoleted or updated. It does not update any of the RFCs it lists, so the core DNSSEC documents still define the protocol.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The core specification of DNSSEC is the combination of RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035. It describes a set of protocols that provide origin authentication of DNS data. RFC 6840 updates and extends them but does not fundamentally change how DNSSEC works.

This document lists RFCs that someone implementing or deploying DNSSEC should consider. It tries to be thorough but does not claim the list is comprehensive. It also points to the relevant IANA registry groups. It does not define terminology and does not point to standards that depend on signed zones, such as DANE (RFC 6698). It does not update any of the RFCs it lists.
sections.plainLanguage: DNSSEC is a big puzzle with lots of separate instruction sheets. This document is the table of contents that tells you which sheets exist.

sections.title: DNSSEC as a Best Current Practice
sections.content:
The RFC states that using the DNSSEC set of protocols is the best current practice for adding origin authentication of DNS data. It adds that, to date, no Standards Track RFCs offer any other method for this.

The text is frank about deployment: more than 15 years after the specification was published it is still not widely deployed. Recent estimates it cites are that fewer than 10% of the domain names used for websites are signed, and only around a third of queries to recursive resolvers are validated. It argues this does not affect best-current-practice status. It only shows that the value of deploying is often considered lower than the cost.

It also points to significant deployment beneath some top-level domains and near-universal deployment for the TLDs in the DNS root zone, as evidence that DNSSEC suits both ordinary and highly sophisticated domain owners.
sections.plainLanguage: Not many people use the seal yet, because it costs effort. But it is still the best way we have, so this document says it is the right thing to do.

sections.title: Advice for Implementers and Operators
sections.content:
Developers and operators of validating resolvers and authoritative servers need to know the parts of DNSSEC that affect them. They should read the core documents and probably at least be familiar with the extensions. Developers will probably need to be very familiar with the algorithm documents too.

The RFC also notes that some DNSSEC-related RFCs have significant errata, so reading them should include looking for the related errata.
sections.plainLanguage: If you build or run DNS servers, read the main sheets and check for corrections to them.

sections.title: The DNSSEC Core Documents
sections.content:
The DNSSEC in use today is the third iteration of the specification. RFC 2065 was the first and RFC 2535 the second, and neither was deployed on a significant scale. Here, DNSSEC means the protocol initially defined in RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

  • RFC 4033 is an overview of DNSSEC, including how it might change the resolution of DNS queries.
  • RFC 4034 specifies the DNS resource records used in DNSSEC.
  • RFC 4035 covers the changes to the DNS protocol: signing zones, serving signed zones, resolving in light of DNSSEC, and authenticating DNSSEC-signed data.

When those were published, an implementation also needed a few older RFCs on cryptography. RFC 2536 covers DSA, which was thinly implemented and can safely be ignored. RFC 3110 covers RSA, still among the most popular signing algorithms. Later RFCs update the core; for example RFC 9077 changes how TTL values are calculated in DNSSEC processing.
sections.plainLanguage: Three main instruction sheets explain what DNSSEC is, what pieces it adds, and how computers should act. A few older sheets describe the secret-code math.

sections.title: RFC 6840 Joins the Core
sections.content:
Over the years developers and operators found issues in the original core documents. RFC 6840 is an omnibus update that has itself become a core document. It covers new requirements from newer DNSSEC RFCs and many security and interoperability issues found in deployment, particularly after the DNS root was signed in 2010. It also lists errors in the examples of the core specifications.

It makes NSEC3 (RFC 5155) as much a part of DNSSEC as NSEC is. It also brings the SHA-256 and SHA-512 hash functions from RFC 4509 and RFC 5702 into the core.
sections.plainLanguage: After people used DNSSEC for a while they found mistakes and gaps, so one big fix-up document was written. It is now treated as part of the main set.

sections.title: Additional Cryptographic Algorithms
sections.content:
Cryptographic algorithms typically weaken over time as computing power improves and new cryptanalysis emerges. Two new signing algorithms have been adopted by the DNSSEC community: ECDSA (RFC 6605) and EdDSA (RFC 8080). Both have become very popular in recent years. The GOST signing algorithm was also adopted but has seen very limited use, likely because it is a national algorithm specific to a very small number of countries.

Developers who want to know which algorithms to implement should refer to RFC 8624. That document is only about what implementations should and should not include. It is not advice about which algorithms zone operators should use to sign or resolver operators should use to validate.
sections.plainLanguage: Secret codes get easier to crack over time, so newer, stronger codes were added. Another document says which codes software should know.

sections.title: Extensions and Further Reading
sections.content:
The DNSSEC community has extended the core and the algorithms with good operational practices and new protocols. The RFC lists these extensions:

  • RFC 5011: automated updates of resolvers' trust anchors. This method was used in 2018 to update the DNS root trust anchor.
  • RFC 6781: a compendium of operational practices.
  • RFC 7344: using CDS and CDNSKEY records to automate maintenance of DS records in the parents of signed zones; RFC 8078 extends it to initial setup of trust between signed parent and child zones.
  • RFC 8198: letting a validating resolver send fewer queries in signed zones using NSEC and NSEC3; RFC 9077 updates it for TTL fields in signed records.

Section 5 adds a list of other documents of interest, including RFC 7583 on key rollover timing, RFC 7646 on Negative Trust Anchors, RFC 8901 on multi-signer models, RFC 9276 on NSEC3 parameter settings and RFC 8499 for DNS terminology. It notes that more related RFCs will certainly be published later.
sections.plainLanguage: People added extras: ways to update the master key, ways to change keys safely, and ways to make answers faster. This part is the list of those extras.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
IANA already has three registry groups related to DNSSEC: DNSSEC algorithm numbers, DNSSEC NSEC3 parameters, and DNSSEC DS RRtype digest algorithms. The rules for the algorithm registry were set in the core RFCs and updated by RFC 6014, RFC 6725 and RFC 9157. This document does not update or create any registries.

For security, the RFC says only that all the security considerations from all the RFCs referenced in it apply.
sections.plainLanguage: The notebooks of code numbers already exist, and this document adds nothing to them. Any safety warnings in the listed documents still apply.
